chapter_theme: Reading what is unspoken from face and eye is the highest social faculty. The chapter places this skill near the divine, treats the eyes that can't do it as useless, and holds that the face betrays what the heart holds.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar divides the chapter: the distinction of those who read signs (701-703), the low standing of those who can't (704-705), the face as the instrument of reading (706-708), and the gaze as its finest instrument (709-710). Chapter 110 has the same title, in the setting of love.

701.reading: One who sees and knows what is meant before it is said is an ornament to the earth, whose waters never fail.
701.nuance: The verse doesn't say whose mind is being read. Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar take it as the king's, Kalaignar as anyone's. After the previous chapter, a minister's skill seems likely, though it is not stated.

702.reading: Regard as equal to a god one who knows, without doubt, what is within.
702.nuance: ஐயப்படாஅது is the claim's high bar: accurate conjecture isn't enough. Parimelazhagar locates the divinity narrowly in this one capacity, while the person stays human in body. Kalaignar's phrase 'if it is said that this power is god's' hedges the verse.

703.reading: Give whatever part of what you have, and gain those who read a sign by a sign.
703.nuance: Parimelazhagar's reading contains a small theory of other minds: since inner workings are alike in all people, knowing one's own gives access to another's. The verse's குறிப்பிற் குறிப்பு is short enough to allow this but does not state it.

positions.position: They read another's sign through their own inner sign; 'parts' are outer possessions such as wealth, land, elephants.
positions.quote: உள் நிகழும் நெறி யாவர்க்கும் ஒத்தலின், பிறர் குறிப்பறிதற்குத் தம் குறிப்புக் கருவியாயிற்று.

positions.position: They read the mind's intent through the sign in the face, and 'parts' can be limbs of the body or of the realm.
They read the face, and the offer is any post in government.
positions.quote: எந்தப் பொறுப்பைக் கொடுத்தாவது துணையாக்கிக் கொள்ள வேண்டும்.

704.reading: Those who take what is meant without its being said and all the others are alike in limbs, yet they are different.
704.nuance: Parimelazhagar completes the thought: lacking the highest knowing, the others are to be classed as beasts. The verse just says வேறு, 'different', and the understatement may be stronger than the gloss.

705.reading: If they can't read a sign by a sign, of what use, among one's limbs, are eyes?
705.nuance: Eyes are asked to do what is not seeing in the ordinary sense. Parimelazhagar says awareness itself is being attributed to the eye here because of how much it helps. Manakkudavar says such people are like the blind.

706.reading: As crystal shows what is near it, the face shows what is strongest in the heart.
706.nuance: பளிங்கு is crystal, and it takes on a neighbouring colour. Pope and Kalaignar's 'mirror' changes the figure: a mirror shows what stands opposite, and crystal changes colour within itself. கடுத்தது is what is most intense, so the face shows peaks and not everything.

707.reading: Is there anything as knowing as the face? Whether one is pleased or angry, it gets there first.
707.nuance: Parimelazhagar treats this as a rejoinder to those who say a face, made of elements, can't know anything, and reads the verse's question as a mock refutation. The point isn't that it knows, but that it arrives before the words do.

708.reading: If you have those who look within and understand what has happened, it's enough to stand and look them in the face.

positions.position: It concerns a petitioner: he need only stand before those who will read his need and resolve it, since speaking shames both.
It's the reverse relation: the king, too, must read his ministers.
It concerns the reader: if he has the skill, he only needs to stand in front of someone.

709.reading: The eye itself will tell of enmity and friendship, if you have those who understand the eye's kinds.
709.nuance: The eye is said to speak (உரைக்கும்), and speech itself isn't needed. Parimelazhagar applies this to foreign kings as read by ministers, so this is diplomatic intelligence at its most subtle.

710.reading: When you look into it, the measuring rod of those who call themselves subtle is nothing but the eye.
710.nuance: என்பார் may carry a slight smile: 'those who say we are fine-minded'. Parimelazhagar explains why the eye: gesture, form, action and speech can all be hidden once one knows they're being read, but a gaze is mixed with the mind. He also records a variant reading, அலைக்குங்கோல்.

links.note: Chapters 71 and 110 share the title குறிப்பறிதல். 709 has the eye say what kings won't, and 1100 says that when lovers' eyes agree, words are useless. A single theory of the speaking eye serves both state intelligence and love, and neither treats speech as the deeper channel.

706 and 710 say the face and eyes can't but show what is within. 585 asks the spy to stand under suspicious eyes and let nothing spill. If the face always reveals, the spy's art should be impossible, and if the spy's art is possible, this chapter overclaims.

Both end with தான்முந்துறும், 'it gets there first'. In 380, fate gets ahead of any plan. In 707, the face gets ahead of any words. 1023 uses it again of a deity. The repeated phrase pictures a force that outruns human intention.

The Kural keeps asking what eyes are for. 577 answers kindly regard, 393 learning, and 705 reading signs. Each makes the physical eye worthless by that chapter's standard, so 'real sight' is defined differently each time.

On Parimelazhagar's reading, the courtier in 698 must treat the king as a god. 702 then gives that same comparison to the man who can read minds, so the servant who can read the god is set beside him.

source_issues: 707: Parimelazhagar's text reads கருதியும் where the parallel with மலர்ந்தும் and Manakkudavar's 706 suggest கருகியும்.
708: Parimelazhagar's explanation reads இறல்பு, likely a typographical error for இயல்பு.
